Women’s Fund Asia and Urgent Action Fund for Women’s Human Rights Asia

description.narrative: Det övergripande målet för samarbetet med Women's Fund Asia (WFA) och Urgent Action Fund, Asia & Pacific (UAF AP) är att stärka bärkraften för feministiska aktivister och organisationer i regionen för att motstå och absorbera motreaktioner; samt att främja de mänskliga rättigheterna för alla kvinnor, flickor och icke-binära personer i Asien och Oceanien.

The overarching goal of the Women's Fund Asia (WFA) and Urgent Action Fund, Asia & Pacific (UAF AP) collaboration is to strengthen the sustainability of feminist activists and organisations in the region to resist and absorb backlash; as well as to advance the human rights of all women, girls and nonbinary persons in Asia and the Pacific.

The overarching goal of the proposed collaboration between WFAs and UAF APs funds is to strengthen the sustainability of feminist activists and organisations in the region to counter backlash; as well as to advance the human rights of all women, girls and nonbinary persons in Asia and the Pacific. The objectives include:
1) Resource defenders, activists and organisations at the frontline of claiming and sustaining of rights of women, girls and non-binary persons 2) Strengthen regional networks, spaces and opportunities for linking, learning and building solidarity 3) Amplify the resource justice advocacy for feminist movements of the Asia and the Pacific region in global funding advocacy spaces

sector.narrative: Women’s rights organisations and movements, and government institutions

description.narrative:
During the reporting period from 1 June 2024 to 31 May 2025, including the 20th anniversary report submitted in January 2026, both WFA and UAF A&P made progress in strengthening the sustainability of feminist activists and organizations across Asia and the Pacific, working to advance the human rights of all women, girls, and nonbinary persons in the region. Through 47 grants across 14 countries, feminist grassroots organisations, activists, and artists have been supported to sustain their rights in increasingly challenging political and financial contexts. Some key highlights of this progress are outlined below.
WFA resourced 34 grants to 32 organisations. Through these, WFA was able to support a wide range of intersecting issues including womens rights, LBTIQ rights, access to justice, environmental justice, SRHR, crisis response, and disability and labour rights. These grants reached key constituencies such as women from marginalised communities, trans and queer people, women workers , and young women and girls. This institutional support builds organisational sustainability by strengthening operational foundations, which in turn enhances the resilience and continuity of the broader grassroots movements they lead and sustain. In addition, through 9 crisis grants WFA was able to respond to a range of crises including the political unrest in Bangladesh; volcanic eruption in Indonesia; floods, landslides, and intense droughts in a hilly district of Nepal; floods in Pakistan. The provisions were in the form of direct relief and essential services, cash assistance, psychosocial support, and capacity building on community resilience. The fund provides flexible support to ensure partners are able to respond timely for rights holders and communities in crisis.
For UAF AP under its Shifting Narratives programme, UAF A&P awarded 13 fellowships to artists and cultural workers from across Asia, with strong representation from queer, trans, Indigenous, and feminist communities. Two major convenings were held: the Regional Convening in Yogyakarta (2024), which brought together 25 artists and researchers to build understanding of cultural rights in movement spaces; and the Crisis & Care Convening in São Paulo (2025), where five artists from the region engaged in cross-movement and philanthropic dialogue. Their practices span drag performance, feminist archiving, visual arts, documentary photography, theatre, and Indigenous storytelling. Through these diverse mediums, fellows interrogate themes such as gender-based violence, intergenerational trauma, environmental degradation, cultural displacement, and the politics of queer survival. The result was the intervention seeded organic collaborations. For example, a queer archivist from Malaysia and a trans photographer from Myanmar began developing a vision for a feminist digital archive to protect artistic expression in hostile environments. Two Indigenous artists from Laos and Malaysia explored how visual and oral storytelling could be used to protect each others communities and foster learning between geographically separated groups. The feedback from fellows has also shown that the programme fills a crucial gap in their access to support, and has helped expand their networks, deepen their practice, and feel less alone in their work. Key takeaway was recognizing how artists form an integral part of the resilience ecosystem within feminist activism. These insights inform not only UAF programme design but also resource mobilization and strategic communications. In line with UAF APs fiveyear strategy (20242029), narrative work has now become central to the organisational approach to feminist protection and sustainability.
